description: A team looking for astrophysics in depth epxloration in order to make a living, public Martian survival and operations map that fuses real-time and archived atmospheric, pressure, radiation, dust, and terrain data into site-specific “survive and operate” recommendations for humans and robots.
summary:
AREOS is a Mars EVA safety companion that helps astronauts stay safe during surface excursions. Before leaving the habitat, the astronaut sets a time limit for their trip to the Mount Sharp boxwork site in Gale Crater. As the clock runs, AREOS continuously monitors radiation, temperature, dust, terrain slope and suit power, using reference values from NASA’s Curiosity rover (RAD and REMS instruments) and Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter HiRISE imagery.
Each reading is rated GO, CAUTION or TURN BACK, and the overall status follows the most serious hazard. The interface changes color, glows and sounds alerts, warning the astronaut 20 minutes before a threshold is crossed. AREOS also checks upcoming checkpoints and recommends a lower bypass route, a slower pace or an early return to the habitat.
To demonstrate how the alerts behave, we have added hazard options such as solar storms, dust storms, cold fronts, rockfall and suit power faults. Sensor values are simulated from NASA reference data rather than a live feed. AREOS turns complex mission data into one clear, instant decision: keep going, be careful, or come home.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?

AREOS is a Mars EVA safety companion that helps an astronaut stay safe during a spacewalk on the surface. Before leaving the habitat, the astronaut sets a time limit for the trip to the Mount Sharp boxwork site in Gale Crater. They also choose a science goal, such as collecting samples, photographing the boxwork ridges or measuring radiation, and a payload weight. The default time limit comes from the suit’s life support, reduced by the payload weight and a safety buffer, and the astronaut can also enter a custom time. As the countdown runs, AREOS tracks radiation, temperature, dust, terrain slope and remaining suit power. Each one is rated GO, CAUTION or TURN BACK, and the overall status always follows the most serious hazard. The status orb, warning bar, screen edge and accent colors shift from teal to amber to red, and the app plays a sound and vibrates the phone. AREOS warns the astronaut 20 minutes before a threshold is crossed. It also looks ahead at each checkpoint on the route and recommends options such as a lower bypass route, a slower pace or an early return to the habitat. To show how alerts behave, we added hazard options for a solar storm, dust storm, cold front, rockfall and suit power fault, so a viewer can watch a solar storm raise radiation until the app says TURN BACK.

What benefits does it have?

The main benefit is that AREOS turns several readings into one clear decision: keep going, be careful or come home. It warns early, so the astronaut has time to act before conditions become dangerous, and it protects the time budget so no one is caught far from the habitat with too little suit life left. Large colors and sounds make it quick to read when the astronaut is busy, and it works offline once loaded, which suits a place with limited connectivity.

What is the intended impact of the project?

Our intended impact is to reduce risk on future Mars missions by making hazard awareness simple and immediate. It is also an educational tool that shows students and the public what an astronaut must watch on Mars, using real NASA reference figures such as the 0.67 mSv/day surface radiation measured by Curiosity’s RAD instrument.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

We built AREOS in VS Code using HTML for the structure, CSS for the design, and plain JavaScript for the timer, hazard calculations, alert logic, route lookahead and screen switching. The route map, gauges and status ring are drawn as SVG in code. We also used browser features: the Web Audio API for alert sounds, the Vibration API for haptic alerts, and local storage to save settings on the device. The type comes from Google Fonts (Chakra Petch and Share Tech Mono). We drew on NASA data and imagery from Curiosity’s RAD and REMS instruments, Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter HiRISE, Mastcam and Navcam, and USGS and JPL maps. No special hardware is needed, because the app runs in an ordinary browser.

How is your project creative?

The project is creative because it turns data into something an astronaut can feel at a glance, with color, glow and sound changing as the danger level changes. The helmet-visor design makes it feel like a real heads-up display rather than a dashboard. It also reasons ahead by checking checkpoints before the astronaut reaches them and proposing alternatives instead of only reporting problems. The hazard options make an idea that is hard to demonstrate, a warning from a Mars sensor, something anyone can try in seconds.

What factors did your team consider?

Our team considered several factors. Safety came first, so the status follows the worst hazard rather than an average, which stops one danger from being hidden by four good readings. We based our figures on NASA sources, but the readings are simulated and the thresholds are illustrative rather than official NASA limits, and the app says so. We designed for use under stress, with large type, strong colors, sound and vibration, and very few steps. We made payload weight affect suit drain, since heavier equipment shortens the safe time. We also considered accessibility and different devices, with a layout that works on phones and larger screens, light and dark themes, and reduced-motion support. Finally, we made it reliable by letting it work offline and show drawn scenes if the NASA photos cannot load.
